4.1.title: Therapeutic indications
4.1.text: Colchicine AGEPHA Pharma is indicated for secondary prevention of atherothrombotic events in adult patients with coronary disease stable for at least 6 months.

4.2.title: Posology and method of administration
4.2.text:
Posology

Adults The recommended dose is 0.5 mg of colchicine once daily. The maximum daily dose is 0.5 mg. The recommended maximum dose must not be exceeded. The initial clinical manifestations of such overdose include gastrointestinal disturbances such as diarrhoea, nausea, and vomiting (see section 4.4). If a dose of colchicine is missed, the missed dose should be taken as soon as possible, and the patient should then return to the normal dosing schedule. If a dose is skipped, the patient should not double the next dose.

Duration of treatment Colchicine can be safely used for a period of 28 months.

Elderly No dose adjustment is necessary. Clinical studies included elderly patients (≥65 years); however, very elderly patients (≥75 years) were under-represented. Available evidence does not indicate a clinically relevant age-related difference in safety or efficacy. As renal impairment, comorbid conditions and concomitant medicines are more common in elderly patients, colchicine should be used with caution in this population.

Renal impairment No dose adjustment is required in patients with mildly decreased (eGFR 60-89 mL/min) or normal renal function (eGFR ≥90 mL/min).

Patients with mildly to moderately decreased renal function with eGFR ≥50 mL/min should be monitored closely for adverse reactions of colchicine. However, colchicine is contraindicated in patients with renal impairment (eGFR <50 mL/min) (see section 4.3).

Hepatic impairment Patients with hepatic impairment should be monitored closely for adverse reactions of colchicine. Colchicine is contraindicated in patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child Pugh C).

Paediatric population There is no relevant use of colchicine in the paediatric population for the indication of secondary prevention of atherothrombotic events in adult patients with coronary disease stable for at least 6 months.

Method of administration

Oral use. The tablet should be swallowed with a glass of water.

4.3.title: Contraindications
4.3.text:
•      Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.
•      Coadministration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or P-glycoprotein inhibitors.
•      Patients with pre-existing blood dyscrasias.
•      Patients with renal impairment (eGFR <50 mL/min).
•      Patients with severe hepatic impairment.

4.4.title: Special warnings and precautions for use
4.4.text:
Important warning Colchicine has a narrow therapeutic index, rendering it susceptible to significant risks of severe overdose. The recommended maximum dose must not be exceeded. The initial clinical manifestations of such overdose include gastrointestinal disturbances such as diarrhoea, nausea, and vomiting. Depending on the dose taken, potential multiple organ failure may ensue, affecting various systems including respiratory, cardiovascular, haematologic, and nervous system. Patients should be made aware of these signs of possible overdosage, which may also occur if interactions are ignored. In this case, a reduction in dose or discontinuation of treatment should be considered. Please refer to sections 4.4, 4.5, 4.8 and 4.9 of this SmPC. The medicinal product must be kept out of reach of others before and after use.

Cardiovascular

The use of colchicine in patients with New York Heart Association (NYHA) Class III or IV heart failure and a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of less than 35% is not supported by clinical efficacy and safety data. Therefore, caution is advised when considering colchicine treatment in this population. Healthcare professionals should carefully assess the potential benefits and risks on an individual basis. For information on other populations excluded from the LoDoCo2 study, refer to Section 5.1.

Blood dyscrasias

Colchicine can cause myelosuppression, leukopenia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopenia, and aplastic anaemia, which can be life-threatening or fatal (see sections 4.3 and 4.8). Gastrointestinal symptoms often are the first sign of colchicine toxicity, so new symptoms should prompt an evaluation for toxicity. Concomitant use of medicinal products that reduce the metabolism of colchicine or the presence of hepatic or renal impairment increases the risk of developing blood dyscrasias.

Use of colchicine in patients with pre-existing blood dyscrasias, renal impairment (eGFR <50 mL/min), or severe hepatic dysfunction, and concomitant use of strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or P-glycoprotein inhibitors is contraindicated (see section 4.3). Concomitant use of moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors with colchicine should be avoided in patients with risk factors for increased systemic exposure of colchicine (see section 4.5). Patients with any degree of renal impairment and hepatic impairment should be monitored for colchicine toxicity.

Neuromuscular toxicity

Colchicine can cause neuromuscular toxicity and rhabdomyolysis. Concomitant use of medicinal products that reduce the metabolism of colchicine or the presence of hepatic or renal impairment increases the risk of developing neuromuscular toxicity.

If a patient develops signs of neuromuscular toxicity, colchicine should be discontinued, other causes should be investigated and treated appropriately. Concomitant use of colchicine and HMG CoA reductase inhibitors, such as atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin and other lipid-lowering medicinal products, gemfibrozil, fibrates and digoxin may potentiate the development of myopathy (see section 4.5).

Patients with any degree of renal impairment should be monitored closely for adverse reactions of colchicine. Colchicine is known to be excreted renally, and the presence of moderate to severe renal impairment has been associated with colchicine toxicity. Urinary clearance of colchicine and its metabolites may be decreased in patients with impaired renal function.

Patients with any degree of hepatic impairment should be monitored closely for adverse reactions of colchicine. Colchicine is metabolized primarily by the liver, and severe hepatic impairment has been associated with colchicine toxicity. Hepatic clearance may be significantly reduced, and plasma half- life prolonged in patients with chronic hepatic impairment.

Women of childbearing potential / Contraception in males and females

Given the mechanism of action of colchicine (see section 5.3), women of childbearing potential should use a highly effective method of contraception while receiving colchicine and for up to one month after end of treatment. Male patients should not father a child during colchicine therapy, and up to 3 months after last dose of treatment. Females using oral contraceptives should be prescribed colchicine with caution and observed for adverse reactions.

Based on non-clinical reproductive toxicity findings and the mechanism of action of colchicine, appropriate contraceptive measures are recommended during treatment (see section 4.6). . Excipient (lactose)

Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose- galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

4.8.title: Undesirable effects
4.8.text:
Summary of the safety profile

Gastrointestinal disorders are the most common adverse reactions with colchicine. These are often the first signs of toxicity and may indicate that treatment needs to be interrupted. These adverse reactions include diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain or cramping.

Historical use of colchicine has been reported to cause neuromuscular toxicity, which may present as muscle pain or weakness (see section 4.4). Serious toxic manifestations associated with colchicine include myelosuppression, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and impairment of renal, hepatic, circulatory, and central nervous systems.

Reporting of suspected adverse reactions

Reporting suspected adverse reactions after authorisation of the medicinal product is important. It allows continued monitoring of the benefit/risk balance of the medicinal product. Healthcare professionals are asked to report any suspected adverse reactions via the national reporting system listed in Appendix V.

5.1.title: Pharmacodynamic properties
5.1.text:
Pharmacotherapeutic group: Antigout preparations, preparations with no effect on uric acid metabolism, ATC code: M04AC01

Mechanism of action

The mechanism of action of colchicine in the prevention of major cardiovascular (CV) events is not understood. Colchicine is considered to act against the inflammatory response by possibly inhibiting the migration of granulocytes to the inflamed area and by interaction with the microtubules, which together could contribute to the prevention of CV events. Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory medicinal product that inhibits microtubule polymerisation and modulates inflammatory pathways implicated in atherosclerosis, including neutrophil activation and the NLRP3 inflammasome. Through these mechanisms, colchicine reduces vascular inflammation, which contributes to residual cardiovascular risk despite optimal standard therapy. . Pharmacodynamic effects

The pharmacodynamics of colchicine in prevention of ischemic cardiovascular events is not completely understood; however, colchicine has been shown to exert cardioprotective, anti-inflammatory and anti- atherosclerotic effects in several animal models in vivo and may stabilize atherosclerotic plaques by reducing inflammatory activity and plaque burden. Favorable plaque-modifying effects of daily 0.5 mg

colchicine therapy, independent of substantial low-density lipoprotein reduction or high-dose statin intensification in patients post-acute coronary syndrome have been observed. Established pharmacodynamic effect (e.g. effect on uric acid metabolism) does not occur at the recommended posology of this product.

Clinical efficacy and safety

LoDoCo2 (ACTRN12614000093684) was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentred trial in patients with chronic, stable coronary artery disease (CAD). A total of 5 522 patients were enrolled, with 2 762 patients assigned to the Colchicine group and 2 760 to the placebo group who underwent median follow-up of 28.6 months. Patients entered the randomized phase only after completing a 30-day open-label run-in period with low-dose colchicine, during which patients with intolerance to colchicine were excluded from randomisation. The patients were required to tolerate colchicine during a pre-randomisation run-in period prior to study entry.

Eligible patients were adults with documented coronary artery disease demonstrated by invasive coronary angiography, computed tomography coronary angiography, or a coronary-artery calcium score of at least 400 Agatston units, who had been clinically stable for at least 6 months. Patients with moderate-to-severe renal impairment, severe heart failure, severe valvular heart disease, or known intolerance to colchicine were excluded.

Baseline characteristics were generally balanced between treatment groups. The mean age of the study population was approximately 66 years, and the majority of patients were male. Most participants had established cardiovascular risk factors and were receiving standard secondary prevention therapy, including lipid-lowering agents and antiplatelet therapy.

The primary efficacy endpoint was the time to first occurrence of a composite of cardiovascular death, spontaneous myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, or ischaemia-driven coronary revascularisation.

Treatment with colchicine significantly reduced the risk of the primary composite cardiovascular endpoint compared with placebo (hazard ratio [HR] 0.69; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.57–0.83; p<0.001), corresponding to a relative risk reduction of approximately 31%.

The interpretation of the efficacy results is subject to several limitations. In LoDoCo2, patients entered the randomised phase only after completing a 30-day open-label run-in period with colchicine, during which patients with early intolerance were excluded. The study population excluded patients with moderate to severe renal impairment, severe heart failure, and other high-risk conditions, which may limit the applicability of results to these populations. Event ascertainment focused on prespecified cardiovascular outcomes, and the collection of non-cardiovascular safety data was limited.

Supportive evidence is available from additional randomised studies and meta-analytic data in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. However, results across cardiovascular trials are heterogeneous, particularly between stable coronary disease and acute myocardial infarction populations. In CLEAR SYNERGY/OASIS-9, a large, randomized trial in patients treated shortly after acute myocardial infarction, colchicine did not significantly reduce the primary composite cardiovascular endpoint. The interpretation of this study differs from stable CAD trials due to differences in population, timing of initiation after acute MI, background acute interventional therapy, adherence considerations and trial conduct during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The clinical benefit of colchicine has therefore been established primarily in patients with stable coronary artery disease.

5.2.title: Pharmacokinetic properties
5.2.text:
Pharmacokinetic studies were conducted in healthy male subjects aged 18-45 years with BMI 18.50- 30.00 kg/m² (N=55 per study) under both fasting and fed conditions.

Absorption

Oral colchicine intake undergoes an entero-hepatic recirculation. In healthy adults, colchicine is absorbed when given orally, reaching a mean Cmax 2.1 ng/ml in approximately 1 hour after a single dose administered under fasting conditions.

The mean absolute bioavailability of colchicine is reported to be approximately 45%.

Effect of food When colchicine was administered with or following a high-fat, high-calorie meal in a bioavailability study, the results showed a lack of a significant food effect. Colchicine may be administered with or without food.

The mean peak plasma concentration of colchicine under fed conditions was found to be 1.8 ng/ml in approximately 1.75 hour.

Distribution

The mean apparent volume of distribution in healthy volunteers is approximately 1300 L. Colchicine binding to serum protein is 39 ± 5%, primarily to albumin regardless of concentration. After reabsorption, is rapidly removed from the plasma and distributed to various tissues. Colchicine is found in high concentrations in leucocytes, kidneys, the liver, and spleen. Colchicine crosses the placenta. Colchicine also distributes into breast milk. Colchicine can also cross the blood-brain barrier and accumulate within the brain, which contains large amount of tubulin.

Biotransformation

Colchicine is demethylated to two primary metabolites, 2-O-demethylcolchicine and 3-O- demethylcolchicine (2- and 3-DMC, respectively) and one minor metabolite, 10-O-demethylcolchicine (also known as colchicine). In vitro studies using human liver microsomes have shown that CYP3A4 is involved in the metabolism of colchicine to 2- and 3-DMC. Plasma levels of these metabolites are (less than 5% of parent drug).

Elimination

In healthy volunteers (n=12), 40 to 65% of 1 mg orally administered colchicine was recovered unchanged in urine. Enterohepatic recirculation and biliary excretion are also postulated to play a role

in colchicine elimination. Following single oral dose of 0.5 mg daily, the mean effective half-life in healthy volunteers is 19 hours. Colchicine is a substrate of P-gp. Colchicine is not removed by hemodialysis.

Renal impairment

No dedicated pharmacokinetic study has been conducted using Colchicine in patients with varying degrees of renal impairment. A published report described the disposition of colchicine (1 mg) in young adult men and women with familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) who had normal renal function or end- stage renal disease requiring dialysis. Patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) had 75% lower colchicine clearance (0.17 vs. 0.73 L/hr/kg) and prolonged plasma elimination half-life (18.8 hours vs. 4.4 hours) as compared to subjects with FMF and normal renal function. In another study, 8 healthy subjects with normal renal function, 8 subjects each with mild, moderate, or severe renal impairment, and 8 subjects with ESRD received a single 0.6 mg dose of colchicine prior to receiving, and again following, haemodialysis. The results showed that colchicine exposure was similar for subjects with normal renal function, mild impairment, or ESRD prior to and during haemodialysis (24.7-31.7 ng·h/mL), but was up to two-fold higher in subjects with moderate or severe renal impairment (48.9 and 48.0 ng·h/mL, respectively). A very small amount of the colchicine dose (mean of 5.2%) was recovered in dialysate.

Hepatic impairment

No dedicated pharmacokinetic study using colchicine has been conducted in patients with varying degrees of hepatic impairment. Published reports on the pharmacokinetics of IV colchicine in patients with severe chronic liver disease, as well as those with alcoholic or primary biliary cirrhosis and normal renal function suggest wide interpatient variability. In some subjects with mild to moderate cirrhosis, the clearance of colchicine is significantly reduced and plasma half-life prolonged compared to healthy subjects. In subjects with primary biliary cirrhosis, no consistent trends were noted. No pharmacokinetic data are available for patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C).

Paediatric population No pharmacokinetics data are available in children.
